title: Cast your care (1 Peter 5:7)
hookLine: cast all your care on him, for he cares for you
last: FEAR NOT COMES WITH A REASON.

lines: CASTING ALL YOUR CARE UPON HIM.
cards: A sticky note on the fridge, half hidden under a magnet: the dentist, the rent, the thing with your sister, the noise the car is making. Lists like that have a way of growing. Cross one thing off and two more appear.

Near the end of a short letter from Peter, written to Christians going through suffering, there's one sentence aimed at that list. In the King James words: "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you."

teach.b: Start with the verb. Cast is not set down politely. It's a throwing word.
The same verb turns up in Luke, when the disciples throw their garments onto a colt for Jesus to ride. A physical motion: off you, onto something else.
Peter ties it to the line just before: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time." In this letter, handing over worry is a kind of humility.
It's admitting you were never built to carry everything. The picture is older than Peter's letter.
Psalm 55 says, "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee." Notice the promise. Not that the burden disappears, but that you'll be held up.
Sustained. Then a story that shows the throw happening.

Hannah longs for a child and has none. At the sanctuary in Shiloh she prays so hard, lips moving and no sound, that the priest Eli thinks she's drunk. She tells him she has "poured out my soul before the LORD."
Eli sends her off in peace. And then the text says: "the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad." Nothing had changed yet.
No child, no answer, no news. But she had thrown it, and she ate her dinner. Last, the reason at the end of Peter's sentence: for he careth for you.
The care you throw lands with someone who cares about you. In English it's the same word, care, going both ways.

how: Christians bring worries to God in private prayer, in prayer journals and on prayer lists, and some churches keep prayer boxes or prayer walls where people leave written requests; 1 Peter 5:7 is often memorized and said in anxious moments.

o: throw your worry onto God, who cares for you
pretend your worries aren't really there
stop caring about the people in your life

games.q: cast your care — tap the pairs.

s: in Psalm 55, casting your burden means it vanishes
the promise is he shall sustain thee: you're held up, not emptied out.
Hannah's sadness lifted before anything had changed
she went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad.
in 1 Peter, cast your care comes right after humble yourselves
humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, then cast all your care upon him.

games.q: you're Hannah. you've poured out your soul at the sanctuary, and the priest Eli has sent you off in peace. nothing has changed yet. what do you do?
o: keep fasting and weeping until something changes.
go your way, eat, and let the sadness lift.
games.why: the woman went her way, and did eat, and her countenance was no more sad. she had handed it over before anything changed.

practice: Take a scrap of paper or open a note on your phone, write one worry in a few plain words, and look at it for a moment. Then fold the paper and set it down out of reach, or close the note.
If you pray, say the verse as you do it, casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you; if you don't, let the motion say: I don't have to hold this every second.

wordCard.voice: Cast your care. Throw your worry onto God, the letter of Peter says, because he cares for you.

orig.note: Greek: worry, anxious care — the 'care' you cast in 1 Peter 5:7.

carryVoice: Your line: he cares for you. Hannah threw it, and then she ate her dinner. That's today, done.
